#10496. McDonald’s has found a new way to sell burgers to people who don’t want to stop playing video games

McDonald’s to gamers: We are so hip.

Ahead of the highly anticipated release of Grand Theft Auto VI last week, the fast food giant announced that U.S.-based gamers can now place an order on Discord to be delivered by Uber Eats. And to demonstrate just how hip the septuagenarian company is, the announcement appealed directly to gamers with text speak—it’s littered with derivatives of “u” in lieu of “you.”

“McDonald’s is showing up on Discord to make it a little easier to get ur McDelivery order when breaking from ur servers just isn’t an option,” the company said in a press release. 

Yes, that’s verbatim from the Chicago-based company—the sort of appeal that could well remind some people of the “How do you do, fellow kids?” meme featuring actor Steve Buscemi from an episode of 30 Rock. Surprisingly, the announcement didn’t elicit many jeers from the Reddit crowd of Discord users, where many people drew comparisons to now-defunct collaborations between fast food chains and gaming consoles that similarly let gamers seamlessly order food. 

Hype around the end of a 13-year wait for a new edition of the popular game surely warranted being a little cringey. The company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment from Fast Company regarding how popular the new ordering option has been thus far, but The New York Times reported that both DoorDash and Uber Eats experienced double-digit spikes in orders in the hours after the game was released. 

MCDONALD’S LATEST MOVES

Even if it’s only a marketing ploy, the Discord ordering optionality illustrates just how much McDonald’s wants to show up for customers. Earlier this month, company executives revealed plans to introduce new value-oriented meal bundles next year to appeal to cash-strapped customers.

And its nearly decade-long collaboration with Uber Eats is nothing to scoff at. Earlier this month, the two companies announced that their nearly decade-long partnership will expand delivery to 14 new markets, adding to its existing 30-country market.

In a more buttoned-up press release intended for investors, Mason Smoot, senior vice president of global franchising and delivery, said its home delivery option—dubbed McDelivery—is a $20 billion-plus global business each year.

Even though the company has been trying for more than a year to overcome a challenging market with its U.S. customers, it’s been making a wide range of attempts to lure them back—and that’s seemingly resonating with investors. 

While McDonald’s shares are still down for the year, they’ve surged more than 14% in the past month. During that same period, the broader S&P 500 Index has slumped nearly 8%.

#10494. Galaxy Z Fold 8 features: What you can do on a foldable

Folding phones have come in numerous variations over the years as the concept has evolved. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the latest evolution that introduces a form factor that fits every user. Its unique design makes it a foldable most people can actually use – which makes it a perfect gift. You might be surprised by what it can do.

It’s in the name. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 folds and unfolds like other foldable devices – that much you know. But what the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s form factor provides is something different to what most might be familiar with.

Instead of a tall device that unfolds into a near-uniform square display, you get a wider screen more like a tablet. That makes it perfect for watching videos or movies. Content that naturally works well on TVs or your computer will look great on the Galaxy Z Fold 8.

What about content that’s best viewed in portrait mode? Because it opens up to a tablet-like display, you can turn the Fold 8 to watch YouTube Shorts or Instagram Reels without a problem, so if you or someone you know likes to watch content on a bigger display, the Z Fold 8 makes that much easier. It really doesn’t matter what content you come across – the wider inner display gives you that large screen feeling.

Like a well-designed tool, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 has more purposes than the tasks best suited for the inner display. That shorter, wider profile makes the outer display smaller, but not as thin as something on other foldables, like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

In reality, the aspect ratio is similar enough across both the inner and outer screens that most content scales well on the shorter front panel. Social apps like X and Instagram look great because videos and images are able to fill the screen, rather than squeeze. Samsung’s One UI software also supports app optimization across both screens, although the experience may vary by app.

Saying the Galaxy Z Fold 8’s outer display is “minimal” isn’t a dig, either. Apps can be refreshing to use when you don’t need to open them on a large scale. Take Messages, for instance. It’s not a complex app, and there isn’t a ton to see – just the last couple of messages exchanged. The same goes for plenty of apps available on the Google Play Store.

And guess what? If you don’t like using the app on a smaller display, just unfold the phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is such a versatile phone, whether it’s a gift during the holidays or one for yourself.

There are instances where you need the large real estate. One UI 9 gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 the option to open and run multiple apps on your screen. There are several ways you can do it, too.

The main approach is to split two apps on the wide inner display. But if you want to see more from one app, you can simply drag the split over in one direction. One UI 9 leaves room to add one more app to that split screen, giving you a three-way Split View. All it takes is dragging an app from the taskbar and choosing the spot.

If you truly need a fourth app open, you have the option to open another in a floating window. Having four apps open at once is definitely a niche instance, but the Galaxy Z Fold 8 handles it like it’s nothing. You can have YouTube up in one corner while you check Messages for gift ideas and shop through the Amazon app. It might be helpful to keep a list of what you got and for whom in a floating Sheets window.

The point is not only that it’s technically possible, but it’s usable. So often devices let users open apps in split screen, but are in no way comfortable enough for the task. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is perfect for it, and the experience actually makes you more productive, not less.

Most phones don’t let you get the best angle without any sort of third-party accessory. The Galaxy Z Fold 8, though, acts like its own tripod in a way.

Let’s say you’re taking photos, and you need to get a shot of yourself, but no one is around to take the photo for you. The Galaxy Z Fold 8’s hinge lets it prop itself up, so you can do things like set a timer and run to strike a pose.

This comes in handy for videos, too. Think of how many times you wanted to get a good angle on a plane or somewhere where there’s this flat surface just asking for a tiny tripod or kickstand. Well, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is its own kickstand and can be positioned at just the right angle.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the leading places to find deals during the holiday season. You’ll find hefty discounts, higher trade-in values for your old devices, and more.

#10493. The state of China's memory industry in 2026

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

A record year for Chinese memory, while Huawei ships its own HBM without a named source.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China’s homegrown memory comes largely from two companies, CXMT for DRAM and YMTC for 3D NAND, and both are booming. CXMT’s Oct. 30 quarterly report shows a nine-month net profit of ¥132.0 billion ($19.6 billion), against a ¥5.28 billion ($785 million) loss a year earlier, on revenue more than eight times as high, at ¥269.0 billion ($40.0 billion). YMTC’s numbers, just for Q1, are at ¥47.04 billion ($7.0 billion) in revenue and ¥33.38 billion ($5.0 billion) in profit attributable to shareholders, more than double 2025.

Both are expanding and adding fabs, and each is edging into the other’s products. No Chinese manufacturer can yet produce high-bandwidth memory (HBM) in volume, though. HBM is the stacked DRAM that AI accelerators depend on, and currently the U.S. bars Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron from selling it into China. CXMT’s prospectus lists no HBM project, though its HBM3E is reportedly in risk production, an early run before the process is fully qualified. Huawei designs its own HBM but doesn’t say who makes it.

Memory is a commodity, so the story is in the wafers. We cover the companies running memory fabs in China: CXMT, YMTC, a handful of smaller Chinese fabs, and Samsung and SK hynix, which run some of their biggest plants there. Huawei makes the cut for its HBM program, though it has no memory fab. Fabless designers, module makers, and NOR flash producers are left out, except XMC for its HBM line. Fab counts, products, and financials come from filings and company statements; capacities, planned fabs, and the HBM progress that remains the big question mark rest largely on anonymous reporting. Let's dive into the current state of the Chinese DRAM industry.

CXMT, short for ChangXin Memory Technologies, is China’s biggest homegrown DRAM maker. It operates two 12-inch fabs in Hefei and one in Beijing, each able to produce around 100,000 wafers a month. It is also building fabs in Shanghai and Hefei and is in funding talks for a second Beijing fab, which together could take it past 600,000 wafers a month. The Shanghai fab is expected to have two to three times the capacity of the Hefei base, with tools going in during the second half of 2026 and volume in 2027.

CXMT is now the fourth-largest DRAM maker worldwide, with 9.5% of DRAM revenue in Q2, according to TrendForce. CXMT says LPDDR6 is in mass production for Xiaomi, and its president says the first 4F² product, a server DDR5 RDIMM, is due by year-end. This comes after record first-half revenue of ¥150.3 billion ($22.4 billion), net profit of ¥77.6 billion ($11.5 billion), an 84.84% gross margin on its main business, and a listing on Shanghai’s STAR Market on July 27. Third-quarter profit alone was ¥54.4 billion ($8.1 billion).

The primary products are DDR5 rated up to 8,000 MT/s with 24Gb dies, and LPDDR5X rated up to 10,667 MT/s. CXMT says its fifth-generation G5 platform reaches 11.95nm active-area half-pitch with quadruple patterning for 24Gb LPDDR5X, and gets at least 50% more dies out of each wafer than G4, counted as 8Gb dies. CXMT says a DRAM product on its sixth-generation platform has also completed engineering-sample validation. Jeongdong Choe, Senior Technology Fellow at TechInsights, told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the firm measured the smallest active half-pitch on CXMT’s G4 at 14.8nm and hasn’t analyzed G5 yet.

CXMT lists no GDDR or 3D NAND among its products and is limited to nodes made without extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography as it lacks the tooling. CXMT’s second Beijing fab, however, is planned to include a 3D NAND R&D line, which could shake things up. The growth picture for now is capacity and price, with the tests of scaling without EUV lying with the RDIMM and Shanghai fab.

YMTC, short for Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., has two fabs of its own in Wuhan, which can produce about 200,000 wafers a month together. A third fab in the Xinzhou district, registered in September last year, is expected to produce about 50,000 wafers a month by 2027 and eventually 100,000 at full capacity. While YMTC is known for its NAND flash, roughly half of Fab 3’s output is earmarked for DRAM. The company also makes enterprise SSDs and UFS and eMMC parts, and sells consumer SSDs under its ZhiTai brand. YMTC filed its own STAR Market prospectus, to match CXMT’s, on Aug. 21.

NAND flash was, until recently, the star of the show for Chinese memory, and YMTC’s Xtacking technology is one reason why. Its fifth-generation Xtacking 4.0 die, used in 1Tb TLC and 2Tb QLC parts, has 294 gates, and Choe told us 267 of them are active word lines. Most of what YMTC ships, however, is still 160- and 232-layer NAND. Samsung licensed YMTC’s Xtacking bonding patents in February 2025, so the technology could be considered both proven and valuable.

Omdia data put YMTC at 38.5% of China’s NAND market in Q2, ahead of Samsung’s 33.5%. Globally, YMTC ranked third in NAND shipments in Q2, according to Counterpoint Research, and its share of NAND revenue rose from 9% to 14% between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026. YMTC’s stated long-term targets are about 20% of global NAND supply and about 500,000 wafers a month, DRAM included.

For DRAM, YMTC’s Fab 2 is running about 5,000 wafers a month of 16Gb LPDDR5, still in R&D and testing, with no plan for mass production. However, a 9,600 MT/s part on a vertical channel transistor (VCT) 4F² cell is slated for mass production at Fab 3 if it passes qualification. XMC, YMTC’s former foundry unit, left its control in July.

Two smaller fabs worthy of note are Fujian Jinhua and SwaySure. The former has a 12-inch fab in Jinjiang, which produces custom DDR4 on 25nm, at 40,000–50,000 wafers a month, with about 90% going to Huawei. DDR4 prices have surged this year, by as much as 50% in the first quarter alone, as the big suppliers wind DDR4 down in favor of server and HBM parts and enterprise buyers stock up.

SwaySure, a Shenzhen company founded in March 2022 with state-owned investment, is building a 28nm 12-inch DRAM line and is reportedly backed by Huawei. Analyst Jim Handy of Objective Analysis doubts the 28nm line could make HBM. Neither company responded to our requests for additional information.

Hefei Phase 1 and Phase 2 (Anhui); Beijing (Yizhuang)

Producing; about 100,000 wafers a month each

DRAM for servers, PCs, and cars, plus HBM lines

Under construction; due by the end of 2026

Hefei under construction; Beijing in funding talks

Producing; about 200,000 wafers a month combined

3D NAND; DRAM planned (9,600 MT/s LPDDR5 on a VCT 4F² cell)

Equipping; starts late 2026 or 2027; about 50,000 wafers a month by 2027

Wuhan, two 12-inch fabs and a reported HBM line

Specialty foundry: NOR flash, MCUs, 3D integration

HBM (a 3,000-wafer-a-month line under construction since February 2024)

Operating; out of YMTC’s control since July 2026

Producing; 40,000 to 50,000 wafers a month

Not every AI chip needs HBM. Inference hardware can get by on LPDDR5X, as Axera’s AX8860P does in Sipeed’s MaixStation, or on DRAM bonded straight onto the processor, the approach PieceMakers is betting on. Training-class accelerators like Huawei’s Ascend series still need HBM, though, and since the U.S. banned the export of HBM as of Dec. 2, 2024, China can’t buy it from the big three memory makers.

Even those who can get HBM are seeing heat and yield issues with larger memory stacks, specifically 12-high. SK hynix said on its Q3 2026 earnings call that some customers’ spec changes show “demand is indeed overwhelming supply,” and that lowering the stack is “a strategy to increase the number of cubes that can be obtained for the same capacity.” This mirrors other indicators, including potential Nvidia Rubin Ultra decisions, and it suggests that HBM is in short enough supply that even easier-to-build stacks are in high demand.

CXMT has sampled HBM with Tongfu, and HBM3 built on its 16nm-class G4 node to Huawei. Its HBM3E has now gone to several domestic AI chip designers as samples, with limited production due by the end of 2026, and an expansion expected in 2027. Yields are only about 20% to 30%, though, against about 70% at SK hynix, and in testing the chips performed closer to SK hynix’s HBM3 than to its HBM3E. An HBM packaging plant in Shanghai worth at least ¥17.1 billion ($2.5 billion) is targeted for year-end, with capacity for about 30,000 units a month.

Tongfu reportedly sampled HBM2, but its own filings mention only DRAM and flash packaging. Huawei said last year that “we will offer two proprietary HBMs.” It launched the Atlas 350 card in March, built on the Ascend 950PR, which carries 112GB of HBM. XMC has had a 3,000-wafer-a-month HBM line under construction since early 2024, but no production has been confirmed. At this time, YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure don’t appear to make HBM, though reports say YMTC is developing the through-silicon via (TSV) stacking it would need, and Jinhua was named in a Huawei-led HBM group in 2024.

Huawei said in 2025 that the 950PR would use HiBL 1.0, its own “low-cost HBM”; TechInsights told us it hasn’t analyzed HiBL 1.0 yet. However, Huawei’s 2025 roadmap specced out the 950PR's 128GB of HBM at 1.6TB/s. Huawei said that its 950PR is “optimized for the prefill stage of inference,” which is compute-heavy with “lower demand for memory access bandwidth,” and that using HiBL 1.0 is “more cost-effective than HBM3E and HBM4E” for that workload. The higher-end HiZQ 2.0, for the 950DT, is due in Q4 and, by Huawei’s figures, brings 144GB at 4TB/s. In both cases, Huawei’s supplier remains in doubt, and the company did not respond to our requests for comment.

HBM3 samples to Huawei; HBM3E sampling, with limited production by year-end at 20–30% yields

Under construction; due by the end of 2026

Shipping since March 2026 in the Atlas 350 (112GB); maker not disclosed

HiZQ 2.0, in the Ascend 950DT (144GB at 4TB/s)

Under construction since February 2024; production not confirmed

HBM samples with CXMT and HBM2 samples reported; filings show only DRAM and flash packaging

Doubtful on a 28nm line (analyst Jim Handy)

Of the companies from outside China, Samsung and SK hynix both run large memory fabs on Chinese soil, and both are now upgrading their NAND lines there. Samsung’s Xi’an handles about 40% of the company’s NAND, including 236-layer, or V8, in volume, with X2 converting to 286-layer, or V9, this year, slated to reach 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December and 40,000 by December 2027. A Samsung spokesperson told Tom’s Hardware Premium that the company “has been transitioning its existing manufacturing operations in Xi’an to 9th-generation V-NAND in compliance with U.S. export regulations and in close communication with the U.S. government.”

SK hynix’s Wuxi produces 30–40% of its DRAM and has moved from 1z to 1a, with the EUV layers done in Korea. Dalian turns out about 100,000 wafers a month of 192-layer floating-gate NAND and is moving to 240 layers, the most SK hynix is authorized to make there.

SK hynix, which already sells NAND with up to 321 layers elsewhere, told us it needs a U.S. license every year and declined to give product details or capacities for individual fabs. The company said that it intends for its 321-layer flash to be “over 50% of domestic (Korean) capacity in the fourth quarter,” which puts the Dalian lag into relief.

SK hynix also has “Mod B,” a second fab at its Dalian site that was completed in 2023. The company has reportedly tied a new U.S. NAND fab to Washington, letting it ship more U.S. tools there: Dalian’s 2026 license capped its equipment, no 2027 license had been issued as of mid-October, and its U.S.-based Solidigm unit has applied for an export license to buy more tools for Mod B. SK hynix told Tom’s Hardware that “no capacity expansion is being sought for the Dalian Mod B” and has been installing equipment at its Dalian factory.

Solidigm is now reportedly in talks with the U.S. Commerce Department over a $45 billion chip plant in the U.S., but wants Washington’s approval to ship equipment to upgrade the Dalian plant first, arguing that the upgrade would help finance the new site. However, SK hynix denied an earlier report of such a deal and says no specific plans have been finalized.

As for its Chongqing packaging plant, SK hynix told us it is “exploring various strategic options to enhance our packaging competitiveness,” though nothing is final. Elsewhere in China, Samsung’s Suzhou plant handles assembly and testing, and Micron’s Xi’an site handles packaging and testing.

All of this plays out inside a U.S.-China fight over chips that AI has only sped up. CXMT isn’t currently on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, which bars U.S. suppliers from shipping to listed companies without a license; YMTC, Jinhua, and SwaySure are. Jinhua has been on the list since 2018; SwaySure joined in December 2024 over its Huawei links, and YMTC was added in December 2022.

CXMT is, however, on the Pentagon’s 1260H list of Chinese military companies, which it is suing over. It’s been on the list since January 2025 and stayed on with the June update. For Samsung and SK hynix, the validated end-user status that let both firms ship in U.S. tools was revoked as of Dec. 31, 2025. Annual licenses are now required, and the Commerce Department has said it doesn’t intend to license capacity expansions or technology upgrades. Meanwhile, both companies say upgrades are under way, which sits uneasily with that policy.

China, for its part, has been weighing broader technology export controls and has now proposed adding 40 technologies, reportedly including some memory-chip design technologies, to its Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export. The draft, Announcement 48 from China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology, is open for comment until Nov. 15, and anyone exporting a listed technology must register first.

About 40% of Samsung’s NAND (both Xi’an fabs)

Converting to V9; 5,000 V9 wafers a month in December 2026, 40,000 by December 2027

DRAM, mostly 1a; EUV layers done in Korea

Floating-gate 3D NAND, 192-layer, moving to 240

About 100,000 wafers a month; 30% to 40% of SK hynix’s NAND

Producing; upgrading, authorized up to 240 layers

Built in 2023; SK hynix says no expansion is sought; no 2027 license yet

Currently, China’s homegrown memory hinges on two manufacturers that are, admittedly, booming at the moment, although the memory industry worldwide has seen a massive surge since spring 2025. SK hynix said that “our DRAM and HBM volume for the next three years through 2029 are effectively sold out” with supply failing to keep up with demand as “a constraint projected to continue through 2030.” Its average selling prices rose from Q2 by mid-20% for NAND and high-20% for DRAM.

There may be some signs of at least temporary cooling in China’s consumer channel, though, as China Flash Market reports that SSD prices fell across the board this week, with most spot NAND wafers trading more than 30% below suppliers’ official prices. It looks like supply will remain a hot topic and China’s production capabilities are front and center.

CXMT and Huawei both have HBM milestones due by year-end: CXMT’s limited HBM3E production and Shanghai packaging plant, and Huawei’s 950DT with HiZQ 2.0. YMTC’s Fab 3 is due in late 2026 or 2027, and CXMT’s HBM3E expansion is expected in 2027. That leaves little time to ramp within 2027, especially at CXMT’s current yields, so we’re skeptical of volume HBM from a Chinese fab, whether measured against domestic demand or global supply, before 2028. Samsung and SK hynix, meanwhile, still need U.S. licenses for next year to keep tooling their Chinese fabs.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

#10492. Ozempic is changing the way Americans shop and eat, even if they’ve never taken it

The new class of drugs led by Ozempic and Wegovy don’t just have transformative effects on the people who take them – they’re reshaping the lives around them too.

Patients prescribed GLP-1s are eating less and drinking less, but those behavioral shifts are trickling down to people in their life who aren’t taking the medications themselves. Nearly one in four U.S. consumers have adjusted the way that they shop, eat, and drink based on knowing other people who take GLP-1s, according to a new survey from market research firm Escalent. 

The survey homed in on a group that the market research group calls “echo consumers,” which refers to people who don’t take a GLP-1 themselves but are changing their habits based on others in their social circles who do. The survey included data from 315 U.S. and 335 U.K. respondents who haven’t taken a GLP-1 drug but know someone who does and report changes to their own behavior based on those social connections.

“Much of the attention surrounding GLP-1 medications has focused on the people taking them, and those living in their households,” Escalent Europe Managing Director Melissa Bane wrote. “… For retailers, food and beverage brands and restaurants, that’s a significant consumer group whose changing habits have gone largely unnoticed.”

Among the echo consumers, 42% reported exercising more, 36% said they consume more wellness products, and 27% are drinking less. When eating out, 49% said they are ordering less at restaurants when eating with someone taking a GLP-1, while 21% are opting for alternative activities instead of socializing while eating and drinking. Almost one in five say they have picked different gifts for GLP-1 users they’ve shopped for, and many say they are buying different food and drinks to bring along to social gatherings in light of smaller appetites and friends and family who aren’t drinking as much.

Industry-shifting numbers

While the new survey only offers a small snapshot of consumer behavior, GLP-1 medications are clearly causing some seismic cultural shifts that we’re only beginning to understand. In the U.S., a massive 11% of the population are currently prescribed GLP-1s and 15% say they have tried them for weight loss before. That huge swath of Americans is already walking, running, and cycling more, buying fewer sweet treats, spending less on groceries, and drinking less alcohol.

Habit shifts among GLP-1 users alone already represent a massive amount of change for industries to adapt to across just a few short years. Beyond those consumers, Escalent’s survey suggests that there are 1.7 times as many people shifting their behavior in light of the widespread use of weight management drugs than there are GLP-1 users. If similar numbers play out in future research, that’s an even more massive chunk of the population suddenly eating, drinking, and buying differently than they did prior to the advent of drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound.

“For Echo Consumers, a box of chocolates or a bottle of wine may no longer be the gift of choice, and social occasions could increasingly revolve around activities rather than going out for food and drink,” Bane said, calling the changes a “major shift” that will be even more evident during the holiday season. 

“Brands, retailers and hospitality businesses will need to find ways to adapt their offerings to reflect changing demand as these habits continue to spread through social networks.”

#10490. Gemini app rolls out very slick camera redesign on Android

Google has thoroughly redesigned Gemini for Android’s in-app camera that lets you quickly add an image to prompts.

Available from the ‘plus’ menu in the prompt box, the old interface launched a fullscreen viewfinder that was quite generic. This UI is still in use when you launch the camera from the Gemini overlay.

The new one appears inline on the Gemini homepage or inside a conversation. It launches as a bottom sheet that you can drag up — with a really slick animation — to take up most of the screen.

This nearly edge-to-edge redesign, which extends behind the system navigation bar, is a stark contrast to the old approach.

To the right of the capture button is a three-dot overflow button that animates on open, revealing options to control the flash and switch to the front-facing camera. There’s a back button on the other side, but you can also just swipe down.

This camera redesign first launched in the Gemini for iOS app, but has now widely rolled out on Android in both the beta and stable (version 17.76+) channels. Be sure to Force stop the Google app if you’re not seeing it live yet.

This follows the launch of GIF creation in the Gemini app yesterday. Powered by Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, select GIF from the Format menu or specify “Create a GIF” in your prompt. Google frames this feature as an alternative to searching for GIFs.

Say hello to GIFs in Gemini. Say goodbye to searching for the perfect one.From looping photo effects to funny memes, create any GIF you can imagine with our latest video model, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, for smooth motion and consistent quality across every frame.

#10488. Major League Baseball sues players’ union ahead of lockout next week

Major League Baseball sued its players’ association in federal court on Wednesday, asking that its contemplated lockout next week be declared legal and trying to head off any attempt by the union to decertify and challenge the work stoppage with an antitrust case.

In a 38-page complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, MLB and the corporate entities owning its 30 teams sued the Major League Baseball Players Association and the eight players on the union’s executive subcommittee, including record-setting pitcher Tarik Skubal.

“MLB brings this action to keep the dispute over the next collective bargaining agreement (‘CBA’) at the bargaining table, where federal law says it belongs,” the lawsuit says. “MLB has a reasonable and imminent fear that the Union will attempt to use the threat of antitrust liability to derail the collective bargaining process altogether in favor of antitrust litigation.”

Baseball’s five-year labor contract expires at 11:59 p.m. Dec. 1 and owners are expected to immediately impose a lockout, which would be the sport’s 10th work stoppage since 1972. Owners have proposed a salary cap for the first time since 1994, when players fought off the proposal with a 7 1/2-month strike that led to the first cancellation of the World Series in 90 years.

Owners asked for a declaratory judgment determining a lockout doesn’t violate antitrust laws and doesn’t amount to an unreasonable restraint of trade. They asked for a ruling that the federal courts lack jurisdiction to enjoin a lockout and for an order that the players be defined as a legal class, which if granted could block individual lawsuits.

“The lawsuit filed today by MLB is completely frivolous,” the union said in a statement. “We will respond appropriately, but MLB’s decision to run to court in the middle of negotiations rather than bargain in good faith is incredibly disappointing.”

Among the lawyers representing MLB are former Solicitor General Paul D. Clement and Keker, Van Nest & Peters, which worked on behalf of the union in litigation against government seizure of drug tests.

“Today’s filing is a defensive measure simply intended to keep the parties at the bargaining table to work towards a new collective bargaining agreement and a full 2027 season,” MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. “We believe the union is preparing to follow the playbook its new leadership has used against other major professional sports leagues by pretending to ‘disclaim’ its status as the players’ bargaining process.”

Caplin referred decertification as a “nuclear option,” mirroring union head Bruce Meyer’s description of the salary cap proposal as a “nuclear bomb.”

—Ronald Blum, AP baseball writer

#10487. The most dangerous election disinformation campaigns

You scrolled through your feed, and a video clip of a candidate’s speech popped up. It doesn’t matter who you planned to vote for, the video struck an emotional—and negative—response. The clip was not AI-generated; the candidate really uttered the words you found upsetting. But the story the video told was fundamentally false. That was the 2026 midterms.

Candidates and their supporters spent a whopping $80 million to make AI-generated ads, as part of what AdImpact projected will be the most expensive election cycle on record. This is one attempt to capture eyeballs and sway voters. Another is through foreign interference. In just one example, researchers tracking a Russian influence operation recently found a fake video masquerading as a Mother Jones report that captured over 11 million views.

But disinformation is not stopping at deepfakes. Authentic videos that are repurposed and stripped of context represent a new frontier. I am not talking about a mere twisting of words. What we’re seeing is next level.

THE NEW LOOK OF DISINFORMATION

Think about the recent catastrophic flooding in Nepal and India. Some footage released within hours of the floods, intended to showcase the magnitude of the disaster, turned out to be from entirely different events. The footage was authentic. It just happened to be from a glacial flood in Alaska, a landslide in Japan, or a flood that occurred years before. These videos racked up millions of views. They also caused panic among friends and relatives trying to find information about their missing loved ones, and they potentially hindered rescue efforts by confusing the locations where help was needed.

Now, consider the same tactic applied in the political sphere—real speeches and words taken drastically out of context, coming from events that could have happened years earlier. 

One of the most notable examples involved Michigan’s recently elected Democratic Senator Abdul El-Sayed. In August, he was eviscerated by Republicans for apparently calling for Sharia law to take over in America. Social media went crazy. Was the clip real? Yes, it was from a speech he gave in 2022. But the meaning was quite different when you look at its entirety in context. So different that Politifact gave it a “pants on fire” rating for its meaning being distorted. 

In Georgia’s hotly contested Senate race, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff ran an ad of Republican Mike Collins urging Americans to get off Social Security and return to work. But that’s not exactly how it went down. The audio came from a broader conversation about tax policy, government revenue, and workforce participation. Collins was not saying retirees should get back into the workforce and lose their benefits (Politifact rated this one as “mostly false”).

In both cases, the recordings were authentic. The misleading impressions came from stripping away the information necessary to understand what was being said, not from manipulating the original material. You may believe that this is just par for the course in a political campaign, but just because something is common does not make it safe, normal, or acceptable. 

THE IMPORTANCE OF CONTEXTUAL UNDERSTANDING

This tactic is becoming effective for two main reasons. Video is now our most prominent data source. Everything is recorded, so if someone is looking for a soundbite to make someone look bad, there is plenty of material available, if they’re willing to dig for it. The second issue is more technical. Deepfake detectors look for signs of manipulation. Authentic videos pass that test. Determining whether a clip is deliberately misleading requires a new set of inquiries, identifying when and where the video took place, what was happening around it, and what the broader context revealed.

Making such determinations traditionally has taken a lot of people a lot of time to dig through archives. Even with the deep war chests candidates possess, they’re not going to devote the human resources needed to debunk every false video, at least not in time for that work to make a dent in the video’s impact. So, campaigns take hits, and candidates can spend considerable time and energy trying to explain past comments and rebuild trust. 

WHAT’S THE FIX?

In 2026, voters and media companies are learning that two things can simultaneously be true: A clip can be legitimate while what it depicts is inaccurate. 

Voters are overwhelmed with election messages. Expecting them to research every clip they see is highly unlikely. Candidates and their backers count on this. Media companies and social platforms bear a greater responsibility, however. Fact-checking and moderation capabilities are essential to reduce the rapid spread of disinformation. Interestingly, while generative AI can be used to create convincing fakes, a different application of AI can be a powerful tool for identifying misleading content and stopping its spread.

As good as AI is getting at generating realistic videos, it’s also getting good at understanding them. Solutions that can read a video and its contextual clues can be indispensable in determining whether an authentic video is being misrepresented online. Imagine an instant army of agent fact-checkers. When AI understands video the way a human does, it recognizes not only what is said and who’s speaking, but what else is on the screen and what the setting looks like. It can also search massive archives to see if that moment has appeared anywhere else. And, at the agent layer, tech can flag suspicious content, assembling supporting evidence and escalating cases to human reviewers in minutes.

The technology that helps media companies and platforms find original footage, restore full context, and flag misleading claims will enable a faster response, not just to political ads but any sort of controversial content that might catch fire. Stopping the spread of disinformation is a perpetual problem. Thankfully, we are now building intelligent tools that can help.

Jae Lee is CEO and cofounder of TwelveLabs.

#10485. The Google Home app is better than Nest alone ever was, mostly

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

The Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest users have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

Having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a big fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That said, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

Google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

The Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

Disagree? What do you think of the Google Home app, and were you still using the Nest app?

#10484. Build Live Video Chat With WebRTC: From First Call to Production Debugging

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Adding real-time video to a web app used to mean plugins, proprietary SDKs and a lot of money. Today every modern browser ships with WebRTC, a set of APIs that lets two browsers exchange audio, video and data directly. The catch is that WebRTC gives you building blocks, not a finished feature. This guide walks through those blocks in the order you actually need them, with the exact API calls you need, and then covers the production issues that tutorials usually skip.

A browser-to-browser call has four moving parts:

Start with the local preview. Browsers only allow camera access on HTTPS or localhost, so serve your page accordingly.

1.     Request a stream with navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia(), passing video constraints (an ideal width of 1280 and height of 720 is a sensible default) and audio constraints with echoCancellation and noiseSuppression enabled.

2.     Assign the returned MediaStream to the srcObject property of your local video element.

3.     Keep a reference to the stream, because you will add its tracks to the peer connection later.

Set the muted and playsinline attributes on the local video element. Without muted users hear themselves, and without playsinline iOS Safari opens the video full screen.

The peers need a way to find each other. A tiny Node.js server using the ws package is enough for development. Its whole job is to relay messages between the peers in a room:

1.     Create a WebSocket server (for example with the ws package) listening on its own port.

2.     Keep a map of room names to the set of sockets in each room.

3.     When a client sends a join message, store the room name on the socket and add it to that room's set.

4.     For every other message type, forward the raw message to the other sockets in the same room, and never echo it back to the sender.

5.     On disconnect, remove the socket from its room so stale peers do not receive messages.

In production you would add authentication, limit room size to two for one-to-one calls, and validate message types, but the shape stays the same.

Both sides create an RTCPeerConnection, add their local tracks and listen for the remote ones:

1.     Create a new RTCPeerConnection with an iceServers list that contains at least one STUN server.

2.     Loop over the local stream's tracks and call addTrack() for each one.

3.     In the ontrack handler, attach the first remote stream to your remote video element.

4.     In the onicecandidate handler, send every new candidate to the other peer through your signalling channel as a candidate message.

One peer creates an offer, the other answers, and both apply each other's descriptions. Candidates arrive asynchronously in the background.

1.     The caller runs createOffer(), applies it with setLocalDescription() and sends the description as an offer message.

2.     The callee applies the offer with setRemoteDescription(), runs createAnswer(), applies it locally and sends it back as an answer.

3.     The caller applies the answer with setRemoteDescription().

4.     Both sides pass every incoming candidate message to addIceCandidate().

If both peers might start a call at the same time, look up the "perfect negotiation" pattern on MDN. It assigns one side as polite and resolves offer collisions cleanly instead of leaving both peers stuck.

On a home network, STUN alone often works. On corporate Wi-Fi, mobile carriers and symmetric NATs it frequently does not, and the call silently fails to connect. A TURN server relays media when a direct path is impossible. The open-source coturn server is the usual choice.

In practice, your iceServers list should contain your own STUN URL plus a TURN URL with a username and credential, so the browser can fall back to the relay automatically when direct connectivity fails.

Generate short-lived TURN credentials on your backend rather than hard-coding them, and budget for bandwidth: relayed calls pass every frame through your server.

Users deny camera access, unplug headsets and switch from Wi-Fi to 4G mid-call. Catch NotAllowedError and show a clear explanation, listen for devicechange events, and use RTCRtpSender.replaceTrack() to swap cameras without renegotiating the whole call.

Listen to pc.onconnectionstatechange. When the state becomes disconnected, wait a few seconds before giving up, because it often recovers. On failed, call pc.restartIce() to try new network paths.

Use RTCRtpSender.setParameters() to cap the bitrate on weak connections, and read pc.getStats() to monitor packet loss and round-trip time. Showing a small "poor connection" indicator does more for perceived quality than any codec tweak.

Mesh calls, where every participant connects to every other, work for two or three people. Beyond that, upload bandwidth explodes. Group calls need a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) such as mediasoup, LiveKit or Janus, which receives each stream once and forwards it to the others.

Tutorials end at a working demo, but the fastest way to understand what production WebRTC looks like is to watch a real call from the inside. Chrome ships an internal diagnostics page that shows every peer connection the browser opens, and it works on any site that uses WebRTC.

1.     Open chrome://webrtc-internals in one tab and keep it open.

2.     In another tab, start a call on your own demo and find its RTCPeerConnection entry.

3.     Expand that entry and look at the ICE candidate pairs: you will see whether the call went direct (host or srflx) or through a TURN relay (relay).

4.     Open the stats graphs for the outbound video stream and watch the bitrate, frame rate and resolution adapt when you throttle the network in DevTools.

5.     Check the negotiated codec and how quickly the connection recovers when you switch Wi-Fi off and back on.

Once you can read your own call, repeat the exercise on a production service. Any browser-based product works, whether a meeting tool or a live video chat that pairs two visitors, because webrtc-internals shows the same data for every site. Expect differences from your demo: more candidate pairs, a relay candidate in the list and a bitrate that adapts faster. Seeing them makes the earlier sections concrete, from why TURN matters to how bandwidth estimation reacts to packet loss.

The one-to-one call above is the core of many products, from telehealth consultations and tutoring to customer support. The engineering challenges grow with the use case: random matching needs queueing and presence on the signalling server, public platforms need moderation and reporting, and global audiences need TURN servers in several regions.

Start with the minimal version, get it working across Chrome, Firefox and Safari on both desktop and mobile, and add TURN before real users arrive. Once the call is reliable, every other feature becomes a much easier problem.

#10482. Workers hoard AI knowledge to stay competitive, Anthropic report says

AI tools are becoming increasingly ubiquitous, but the best techniques for using them are likely still a secret.

This is because workers who develop highly effective AI tricks have no incentive to share them with their colleagues or their bosses, notes a report published Monday by Anthropic.

Researchers interviewed 66 executives, managers, and employees at 58 of Anthropic’s corporate customers and found that many workers are reluctant to share their best AI tricks, citing reasons ranging from job security to more leisure time.

The practice has frustrated managers looking to exploit AI-driven efficiencies. The report quotes one exasperated executive saying, “They don’t want you to know, because they want to use those 10 hours a week to go walk their dog.”

AI hoarding is a new form of the age-old workplace phenomenon of knowledge hiding, in which employees deliberately withhold information from their coworkers to retain a competitive edge.  

Employees in the AI age have even more at stake: their jobs. If the trick they develop is powerful enough, they might render themselves redundant. And even for those whose jobs are secure, revealing a time-saving trick might just mean they are assigned more work.

That raises a thorny question for business leaders: How do you incentivize employees to help automate their own jobs?

Employers hoping to discourage AI hoarding may need to rethink how they measure and reward productivity. Otherwise, employees might realize that their most valuable professional asset is something they’re better off keeping secret.

#10481. Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 vs Watch 9: When is it right to spend more?

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

As we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

That shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

The clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

The Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:

Choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

If you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling new generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

#10478. Innovation doesn’t scale on its own

I’ve traveled to communities experiencing severe acute malnutrition, and what stays with me is what I didn’t hear.

Anyone who has spent time around young children knows the noise—the laughter, the crying, the constant motion. When malnutrition has reached a crisis point, that noise is gone. Children sit still in ways they aren’t supposed to.  

That stillness is one of the first signals something is wrong. Intervening early is critical. Health workers can use the most basic tools to measure a child’s upper arm to quickly assess nutritional health. 

The intervention is surprisingly simple: providing a small packet filled with peanut paste, milk powder, and a precise blend of micronutrients. A six-week course of the packets follows and it can alter the entire trajectory of their life.

Thirty years later, it remains one of the world’s most effective tools in global health.

WHY PRODUCT INNOVATION ISN’T ENOUGH

There’s a persistent bias toward the new in how innovation gets funded. Moonshots are celebrated and disruption gets rewarded. The assumption is that the most transformative solutions involve the most sophisticated technology.

Breakthrough innovation is important, but collective expertise, commitment, and coordination are critical to scaling. 

Ready-to-use therapeutic food, known as RUTF, is one of these breakthrough innovations. Before it existed, treating severe acute malnutrition meant hospital stays and clinical formulas most families couldn’t access. RUTF changed the equation with a shelf-stable, portable product that didn’t require refrigeration. A caregiver could administer it at home. A health worker could distribute it in a village with no running water.

Its success was never tied to a single organization. Over the past three decades, it has been adopted by governments, humanitarian organizations, and health systems around the world.

For business leaders, the lesson is familiar. The challenge is rarely inventing the solution. It’s building the conditions that allow it to scale.

THE OVERLOOKED NECESSITY

We often think of innovation as a product challenge. Build the right solution and impact follows. But scale rarely works that way.

What determines success is everything surrounding the innovation: distribution, financing, trust, incentives, and infrastructure.

Getting RUTF to a child who needs it is more than a point A to point B challenge. It requires identifying malnutrition before it becomes irreversible, especially in the first 1,000 days of life. It necessitates a health worker who can make that call—and in many communities, that person isn’t a credentialed clinician. It is often a minimally compensated local community member. 

It requires supply chains that reach remote places where businesses don’t. It depends on coordination between governments, manufacturers, and health systems. If any one of those fails, a child goes untreated.

RUTF endures because the ecosystem built around it proved strong enough to sustain it through political shifts, funding disruptions, and supply chain crises. That infrastructure is consistently underestimated and consistently underfunded.

THE NEXT INNOVATION

The next breakthrough for nutrition is a systems innovation—one that closes the gap between what works and what reaches people at scale.

The UNICEF-led Child Nutrition Fund puts that idea into action. By bringing together government leadership, financing, and technical expertise, it helps accelerate the scale-up of proven nutrition interventions while strengthening the systems behind them. In doing so, it helps bridge critical gaps in nutrition services and supports country-led efforts to save lives, build resilience, and improve outcomes for women and children.

That’s the innovation this moment requires—a smarter way to build and sustain the systems that deliver it.

Don’t just back a product. Back the infrastructure that makes it possible. The right product can change a child’s life. The ecosystem is what gets it there, and scale is what reshapes the future.

The leaders who understand this invest in the breakthroughs and the systems that make breakthroughs last.

Michele Walsh is executive vice president and chief philanthropy officer of UNICEF USA.

#10475. Screen time got your brain fried? Try a ‘brain stack’

Every few months, like clockwork, a new analog trend emerges in an effort to get us all off our phones. . .and of course, document the process for social media. 

The latest is “brain stacking”: keeping a stack of puzzle books, novels, non-fiction and other phone-free activities in a neat pile within arm’s reach, in lieu of doomscrolling. 

Online, thousands of people have proudly shared their “stacks”. One popular creator, Mandy Rulez, regularly shares timelapse videos of her brain stacks before work, starting her morning with nearby stacks of non-digital activities, like journaling, before moving on to a sudoku, a crossword, and finally a quick ten pages of reading. 

Other creators are also incorporating timers into the mix. For example, a 12-minute brain dump in a spiral notebook, followed by ten minutes of planning, 15 minutes of puzzles, 20 minutes of coloring. Total brain stack: one hour.  

Brain stacking is a continuation of the “analog bag” trend earlier this year (otherwise known as, well, simply “doing things.”) But we’re in an era when “brain rot” and “doomscrolling” have become part of our everyday lexicon, so it’s easy to see the appeal. Gen Z, after all, are the ones embracing dumb phones and buying up Bricks in an effort to reduce their screen time.

The idea of “habit stacking” has existed in the world of self-help for years, and involves stacking new habits to existing ones. More recently, bedtime stacking, as well as peptide stacking, have emerged as online trends. Then there’s goal stacking and income stacking. Clearly, queuing up back-to-back activities (and, ideally, literally and physically stacking them in a pile to work through) resonates with people on social media.

In a year where “maxxing” was crowned Dictionary.com’s word of the year, it’s unsurprising that a single activity alone is not enough—instead, we must stack them one on top of each other to reach our max potential. (There is also the visually pleasing element of the stack when it comes to posting online.) 

That does not mean there’s anything inherently wrong with brain stacking. Having a range of activities close at hand means you are far more likely to be intentional with your spare time. 

And a 2024 study found just five minutes of fiction reading can reduce stress by up to 20%, as well as sharpening concentration and problem-solving skills. Reading is also associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease. 

But recent findings from a collaboration among researchers at Clemson University, the Medical University of South Carolina, and Penn State found that “brain-training” activities, such as crosswords, sudoku, memory games and adult coloring books, are not equally effective for everyone. 

College students, for example, often show only modest benefits from such brain-training activities compared with older adults who live relatively sedentary lifestyles. There’s also no specific research that supports the brain stacking method of working your way through a queue of a certain number of tasks, or spending a specific amount of time on each.

If you find yourself absorbed in a book, or reach a flow state in your writing, don’t feel bound to 10-minute sprints and then moving onto the next brain-boosting activity. 

That said? Any amount of time away from your screens is time well spent.

#10474. Which Samsung folding phone is right for you? Galaxy Z Fold 8, Ultra, or Flip 8

Folding phones are entering a new chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most important questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

Samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the new kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:

Starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most important priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

When it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That said, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

In either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

One of the most important things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra.

Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

If you are moving into a new Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

#10471. Building Email Integrations: APIs, Webhooks, Automation, and Deliverability

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Email remains an important communication channel for web applications. From account verification and password resets to product announcements and customer notifications, many applications depend on email to keep users informed.

For developers, however, implementing email functionality involves more than connecting a service and sending a message. A reliable email system needs to handle authentication, dynamic content, delivery failures, user preferences, event tracking, and integrations with other application components.

Using an email service provider (ESP) can simplify this process. Most modern providers offer REST APIs, SMTP relays, templates, automation features, and reporting tools that developers can integrate into existing applications.

This guide explores the technical considerations involved in building email integrations, including API-based sending, webhook handling, automation workflows, and deliverability.

There are two common ways to connect an application to an email delivery service: SMTP and REST APIs.

SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is a standard protocol used to transfer email messages between servers. Developers can connect an application to an SMTP server using credentials and configuration settings.

REST APIs provide another approach. Instead of communicating through an email server protocol, an application sends HTTP requests to an endpoint. The provider processes the request and returns a response.

Both methods can support transactional and application-generated emails, but their implementation differs.

An application already supports SMTP configuration.

Developers want a relatively straightforward integration.

Existing frameworks or libraries provide built-in SMTP support.

An application needs programmatic control over email operations.

Developers want structured responses and error handling.

Email functionality needs to integrate with other application services.

The system requires event tracking or additional API capabilities.

The right approach depends on the application's architecture, expected email volume, and integration requirements.

An API integration allows an application to trigger emails in response to specific events.

For example, an ecommerce application might send an order confirmation after a successful payment. A SaaS application could send an account verification message after registration.

A typical integration follows this process:

The backend prepares the recipient and message data.

The backend authenticates with the email provider.

The application records the response and handles any errors.

Consider a Node.js application that needs to trigger an email campaign through an API.

Some platforms, including Mailmodo, provide REST API functionality for triggering campaigns and integrating external applications with email workflows.

The following example demonstrates the general structure of an HTTP request using a campaign-triggering endpoint:

This example uses the documented Mailmodo trigger endpoint and request structure. The campaign ID and API key must be replaced with the values from the relevant account.

Notice that the API key is loaded from an environment variable rather than written directly into the source code.

This is an important security practice. Credentials should never be exposed in frontend JavaScript, public repositories, or client-side application bundles.

Not every email provider offers the same integration capabilities. Developers should evaluate providers based on their API documentation, authentication methods, supported endpoints, event notifications, and integration flexibility.

For example, Elastic Email provides a REST API that developers can use to send emails and manage different email operations from an application.

Its API uses HTTPS requests and API-key authentication. Developers can use the available endpoints to send messages, manage campaigns, retrieve information, and configure webhook notifications.

When evaluating an email API, consider these technical requirements:

Authentication: Check how API keys are generated, stored, restricted, and rotated.

Documentation: Look for clear endpoint descriptions, request examples, response formats, and error codes.

SDK availability: Official libraries can reduce the amount of integration code required.

Permission management: Separate credentials for sending emails and accessing account information can reduce unnecessary exposure.

API limitations: Review connection limits, request timeouts, rate limits, and account-level restrictions before deploying an integration.

A provider with extensive features is not necessarily the best option for every project. The important consideration is whether its API supports the application's actual requirements.

Sending an email is only one part of the communication process. Applications may also need to know what happens after a message is submitted.

A webhook allows an external service to send an HTTP notification to an application when a particular event occurs.

Depending on the provider, events may include:

For example, an application could receive a delivery-failure notification and update the corresponding email record in its database.

A basic Express.js webhook endpoint might look like this:

This is a simplified example rather than a complete provider-specific webhook implementation. A production endpoint should validate the provider's signature or other authentication mechanism and follow its documented payload structure.

It should also handle duplicate events safely. Webhook providers may retry notifications when an application does not respond successfully.

An idempotent event handler prevents the same notification from creating duplicate database updates or triggering repeated actions.

Email automation connects application events with predefined communication sequences.

Instead of manually sending every message, developers can create workflows that respond to user activity.

Consider a SaaS application with the following registration process:

If the user does not complete onboarding, a follow-up message may be triggered.

A simplified workflow can be represented as:

In a production application, email delivery should generally be handled through a background job queue rather than blocking the registration request.

A queue also makes it easier to retry temporary failures, manage sending volume, and prevent email delays from affecting the main application.

Developers should consider tools such as Redis-backed queues or framework-specific job processors when building larger systems.

Automation platforms can also help manage more complex journeys. For instance, a developer can connect application events to an external email workflow instead of implementing every communication sequence independently.

The key is to keep business logic in the application while using the email service to manage message delivery and relevant campaign operations.

A successful API response does not necessarily mean that an email has reached the recipient's inbox.

Email deliverability depends on several technical factors, including domain authentication, sender reputation, message quality, and recipient engagement.

Developers should pay attention to the following configurations.

Sender Policy Framework identifies the mail servers authorized to send messages on behalf of a domain.

A correctly configured SPF record helps receiving servers evaluate whether an email originates from an authorized source.

DomainKeys Identified Mail adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages. Receiving servers can use the corresponding public key in DNS to verify the signature.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance builds on SPF and DKIM. It allows domain owners to publish policies for handling messages that fail authentication checks and receive reports about authentication activity.

These three mechanisms should be configured carefully, especially when an application sends emails through multiple providers.

Email systems generate useful operational data. However, developers should avoid treating every available metric as an accurate measure of user engagement.

More reliable application-level signals can include:

These events can be connected with email campaign data to understand how communication affects application activity.

Developers should also maintain a clear separation between email delivery records and user account records. This makes it easier to investigate delivery issues without unnecessarily modifying customer data.

Before deploying an email integration, developers should review the following areas:

API security: Store credentials in environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager.

Domain authentication: Configure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

Error handling: Account for failed requests, invalid recipients, and temporary provider errors.

Background processing: Use queues for asynchronous email delivery.

Webhook validation: Verify incoming notifications and handle duplicate events.

Monitoring: Track delivery failures, bounce rates, and application-level outcomes.

Testing: Test email templates across different clients and devices before production deployment.

These practices help create an email system that is easier to maintain, troubleshoot, and scale.

Email integration is an important part of modern application development, but a reliable implementation requires more than connecting an SMTP server or calling an API endpoint.

Developers need to consider authentication, asynchronous processing, webhook security, automation logic, domain configuration, and event monitoring.

REST APIs are useful for applications that need programmatic control over email operations, while SMTP remains a practical option for systems that already support standard mail-server connections. Webhooks add another layer by allowing applications to respond to delivery events and update their internal records.

By choosing an integration method that fits the application architecture and following sound security and deliverability practices, developers can build email functionality that supports both immediate communication needs and long-term application growth.

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very quickly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a big part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for important apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.
